HW5 - Annie Sherwood¶

Dataset: day_missing.csv - the UCI Bike Sharing daily data set (Capital Bikeshare, Washington D.C., 2011-2012) with some values removed and some outliers injected.

Each row is one day. Key columns (from the UCI data documentation):

column meaning
dteday date
season season code (mapping derived from the data below)
weathersit 1 = Clear / few clouds, 2 = Mist / cloudy, 3 = Light rain or snow, 4 = Heavy rain / snow / fog
temp, atemp normalized temperature and "feels-like" temperature
hum, windspeed normalized humidity and wind speed
casual, registered, cnt casual riders, registered riders, total riders
workingday 1 = neither weekend nor holiday, else 0

The notebook is meant to be run top-to-bottom; each question builds on the DataFrame produced by the previous one.

Setup - imports and shared constants¶

In [1]:
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

DATA_FILE = 'day_missing.csv'

# Fixed categorical colour order (blue, orange, aqua, yellow) so that a
# category always keeps the same colour across every chart.
PALETTE = ['#2a78d6', '#eb6834', '#1baf7a', '#eda100']

# Weather-situation names from the UCI Bike Sharing documentation.
WEATHER_NAMES = {
    1: 'Clear',
    2: 'Mist',
    3: 'Light Rain or Snow',
    4: 'Heavy Rain or Snow',
}

sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid')

Data inspection¶

Required first output, in order: shape, dtypes, missing values per column, the sorted unique values of season and weathersit, and the evidence for the season mapping.

# ... and the calendar dates on which each code starts and ends.
dates = pd.to_datetime(df['dteday'], format='%m/%d/%Y')
day_of_year = dates.dt.strftime('%m-%d')
print('\nMonth-day range covered by each season code:')
print(day_of_year.groupby(df['season']).agg(['min', 'max']))

# Codes 1-3 never wrap the year, so min/max show their exact boundaries.
# Code 1 covers January, so its December days are the ones after the
# season-4 days end.
for code_value in sorted(df['season'].unique()):
    in_season = dates[df['season'] == code_value]
    runs = in_season.diff().dt.days.ne(1).cumsum()
    first_run = in_season.groupby(runs).agg(['min', 'max']).iloc[0]
    print(f'season {code_value}: first run '
          f'{first_run["min"]:%Y-%m-%d} to {first_run["max"]:%Y-%m-%d}')

Reading the evidence. Code 1 holds all of January and February, the first ~20 days of March and the last ~10 days of December. Code 2 starts around 21 March and runs to around 20 June; code 3 runs from about 21 June to about 22 September; code 4 from about 23 September to about 20 December. Those boundaries are the astronomical equinoxes and solstices, so:

  • 1 = Winter (21 Dec - 20 Mar)
  • 2 = Spring (21 Mar - 20 Jun)
  • 3 = Summer (21 Jun - 22 Sep)
  • 4 = Fall (23 Sep - 20 Dec)

The mapping below is built from the data: each code is labelled by the month it covers most often, and that month is translated to its astronomical season.

In [3]:
# Month that falls inside each season code most often.
dominant_month = pd.crosstab(df['season'], df['mnth']).idxmax(axis=1)

# Northern-hemisphere astronomical season each whole month belongs to.
MONTH_TO_SEASON = {
    1: 'Winter', 2: 'Winter', 3: 'Spring', 4: 'Spring', 5: 'Spring',
    6: 'Summer', 7: 'Summer', 8: 'Summer', 9: 'Fall', 10: 'Fall',
    11: 'Fall', 12: 'Winter',
}

SEASON_NAMES = {
    int(code_value): MONTH_TO_SEASON[month]
    for code_value, month in dominant_month.items()
}
print('Dominant month per season code:', dominant_month.to_dict())
print('Season mapping:', SEASON_NAMES)

WEATHER_PRESENT = {
    int(code_value): WEATHER_NAMES[code_value]
    for code_value in sorted(df['weathersit'].unique())
}
print('Weather mapping (codes present in the data):', WEATHER_PRESENT)

Dominant month per season code: {1: 1, 2: 5, 3: 7, 4: 10}
Season mapping: {1: 'Winter', 2: 'Spring', 3: 'Summer', 4: 'Fall'}
Weather mapping (codes present in the data): {1: 'Clear', 2: 'Mist', 3: 'Light Rain or Snow'}

Note that weathersit only takes the values 1, 2 and 3 - there are no Heavy Rain or Snow (code 4) days in this data, so charts that use weathersit show three categories.

Q1. Four-moment table¶

A column qualifies when it is numeric and has more than 8 distinct non-missing values. Applied strictly, this selects instant (a row counter) and mnth (12 values) as well as the measured variables; they are kept because the rule says so, although they are not meaningful continuous measurements.

Kurtosis is Fisher's (excess) kurtosis - a normal distribution scores 0. pandas' .kurt() uses that definition and skips missing values.

In [4]:
numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes(include='number').columns
continuous_cols = [col for col in numeric_cols if df[col].nunique() > 8]
print('Columns with more than 8 distinct values:', continuous_cols)

moments = pd.DataFrame({
    'mean': df[continuous_cols].mean(),
    'std': df[continuous_cols].std(),
    'skew': df[continuous_cols].skew(),
    'kurtosis': df[continuous_cols].kurt(),
}).round(4)

Q2. Kurtosis flag for possible outliers (|kurtosis| > 1.8)¶

In [5]:
KURTOSIS_LIMIT = 1.8

flagged = moments.loc[moments['kurtosis'].abs() > KURTOSIS_LIMIT, 'kurtosis']
if flagged.empty:
    print(f'No variable has |kurtosis| > {KURTOSIS_LIMIT}.')
else:
    print(f'Variables with |kurtosis| > {KURTOSIS_LIMIT}:',
          flagged.index.tolist())
    print(flagged.to_string())

Variables with |kurtosis| > 1.8: ['temp']
temp    162.4505

The flagged variables have tails heavier than the threshold allows, which suggests outliers. temp is the clearest case: its maximum is far outside the 0-1 normalized range the rest of the column uses.

Q3. Outliers set to missing (2.1 x IQR rule)¶

For each Q1 column: Q1 and Q3 are the 25th and 75th percentiles, IQR = Q3 - Q1, and a value is an outlier if it is below Q1 - 2.1 x IQR or above Q3 + 2.1 x IQR. The fences are computed by hand from the quantiles; outliers are replaced with np.nan.

In [6]:
IQR_MULTIPLIER = 2.1

outlier_counts = {}
for col in continuous_cols:
    q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
    q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lower_fence = q1 - IQR_MULTIPLIER * iqr
    upper_fence = q3 + IQR_MULTIPLIER * iqr

    # Comparisons with NaN are False, so existing gaps are not counted.
    is_outlier = (df[col] < lower_fence) | (df[col] > upper_fence)
    outlier_counts[col] = int(is_outlier.sum())
    if is_outlier.any():
        df.loc[is_outlier, col] = np.nan

outlier_table = (
    pd.Series(outlier_counts, name='outliers_replaced')
    .rename_axis('variable')
    .loc[lambda counts: counts > 0]
    .to_frame()
)
outlier_table
Out[6]:
outliers_replaced

hum 1
windspeed 1

Q4. Mean imputation (only the columns changed in Q3)¶

Only the columns listed in the Q3 table are imputed, each with the mean of its remaining values (the post-Q3 mean). Other columns keep their original missing values.

In [7]:
treated_cols = outlier_table.index.tolist()

post_q3_means = df[treated_cols].mean()
df[treated_cols] = df[treated_cols].fillna(post_q3_means)

Q5. Post-imputation kurtosis check¶

In [8]:
kurtosis_check = pd.DataFrame({
    'kurtosis_before': moments.loc[treated_cols, 'kurtosis'],
    'kurtosis_after': df[treated_cols].kurt().round(4),
})
kurtosis_check['difference'] = (
    kurtosis_check['kurtosis_after'] - kurtosis_check['kurtosis_before']
).round(4)
kurtosis_check = kurtosis_check.sort_values(
    'difference', key=np.abs, ascending=False
)
kurtosis_check

In [9]:
biggest = kurtosis_check.index[0]
change = kurtosis_check.loc[biggest, 'difference']
direction = 'lighter' if change < 0 else 'heavier'
print(f'Largest change: {biggest} ({change:+.4f}); tails became {direction}.')

still_high = df[continuous_cols].kurt()
still_high = still_high[still_high.abs() > KURTOSIS_LIMIT].round(4)
if still_high.empty:
    print(f'After treatment, no column has |kurtosis| > {KURTOSIS_LIMIT}.')
else:
    print(f'Columns still above |kurtosis| > {KURTOSIS_LIMIT}:')
    print(still_high.to_string())

Largest change: temp (-163.5116); tails became lighter.
After treatment, no column has |kurtosis| > 1.8.

Interpretation. temp changed the most. Its kurtosis fell from a very large positive value (162.45) (a handful of impossible readings such as 58.75 on a 0-1 scale) to a negative value (-1.06), so its tails became much lighter - after the extreme values were replaced with the mean, the distribution is flatter than a normal one, which is what a seasonal temperature series looks like. The other treated columns moved by much smaller amounts, also toward lighter tails. The printout above shows whether any column still exceeds the 1.8 threshold after treatment.

Q9. Casual vs. registered riders with marginal histograms¶

seaborn.JointGrid draws the scatter plot in the centre and a histogram of each variable in the margins; both are split by workingday.

In [13]:
joint_df = df[['casual', 'registered']].copy()
joint_df['Day type'] = df['workingday'].map(
    {0: 'Weekend / holiday (0)', 1: 'Working day (1)'}
)
day_order = ['Working day (1)', 'Weekend / holiday (0)']

joint = sns.JointGrid(
    data=joint_df,
    x='casual',
    y='registered',
    hue='Day type',
    hue_order=day_order,
    palette=PALETTE[:2],
    height=7,
)
joint.plot_joint(sns.scatterplot, s=18, alpha=0.7, edgecolor='none')
joint.plot_marginals(sns.histplot, bins=30, alpha=0.5, element='step')
joint.set_axis_labels('Casual riders per day', 'Registered riders per day')
joint.ax_joint.legend(title='Day type', loc='lower right')
joint.figure.suptitle('Casual vs. registered daily riders', y=1.02)
plt.show()

Working days are dominated by registered (commuter) riders, while weekends and holidays attract many more casual riders for a similar number of registered riders.

Q10. Treemap of total riders by weather situation¶

One rectangle per weathersit value present in the data, sized by the sum of cnt, labelled with the weather name and its total, each in its own colour.

In [14]:
weather_totals = df.groupby('weathersit')['cnt'].sum().sort_values(
    ascending=False
)
labels = [
    f'{WEATHER_PRESENT[code_value]}\n{total:,.0f} rides'
    for code_value, total in weather_totals.items()
]
colours = [PALETTE[code_value - 1] for code_value in weather_totals.index]



def treemap_layout(sizes, x, y, width, height, gap=0.8):
    """Return one (x, y, w, h) rectangle per size, areas proportional.

    Each rectangle takes its share off the longer side of the space left
    over, then the rest is laid out the same way (slice-and-dice).
    """
    rects = []
    remaining = float(sum(sizes))
    for size in sizes:
        share = size / remaining
        if width >= height:
            w = width * share
            rects.append((x, y, w, height))
            x, width = x + w, width - w
        else:
            h = height * share
            rects.append((x, y, width, h))
            y, height = y + h, height - h
        remaining -= size
    # Shrink each rectangle slightly so neighbours are separated by a gap.
    return [(rx + gap / 2, ry + gap / 2, rw - gap, rh - gap)
            for rx, ry, rw, rh in rects]


CANVAS = 100
rects = treemap_layout(list(weather_totals.values), 0, 0, CANVAS, CANVAS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6.5))
for (rx, ry, rw, rh), label, colour in zip(rects, labels, colours):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle(
        (rx, ry), rw, rh,
        facecolor=colour, label=label.replace('\n', ' - '),
    ))
    centre_x = rx + rw / 2
    centre_y = ry + rh / 2
    if min(rw, rh) > 10:
        ax.text(centre_x, centre_y, label, ha='center', va='center',
                color='white', fontsize=12, weight='bold')
    else:
        # Too thin to hold text: label it just outside with a pointer.
        ax.annotate(label.replace('\n', ' - '), xy=(centre_x, centre_y),
                    xytext=(centre_x, CANVAS + 6), ha='center',
                    fontsize=11, weight='bold',
                    arrowprops={'arrowstyle': '-', 'color': '0.3'})

ax.set_xlim(0, CANVAS)
ax.set_ylim(0, CANVAS + 10)
ax.legend(loc='upper center', bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.02), ncol=3,
          frameon=False, title='Weather situation')
ax.set_title('Total bike rentals by weather situation (2011-2012)')
ax.axis('off')
plt.show()

Clear days account for most rides, misty days for most of the rest, and light rain or snow for only a small share; heavy rain or snow never occurs in this data set, so it has no rectangle.
